lesson.title: When One Structure Is Not Enough: Introducing Resonance
lesson.summary: Resonance structures are two or more valid Lewis structures for the same molecule that differ only in the placement of electrons, used together to describe molecules whose real bonding is not accurately captured by any single structure.
lesson.body:
Sometimes a molecule can be drawn with more than one valid Lewis structure, all with the same atoms in the same positions and the same total number of electrons, but with double bonds and lone pairs distributed differently. When this happens, no single one of those structures is correct on its own. Chemists call this set of structures resonance structures, and the real molecule is best understood as a blend of all of them, not as one structure or the other, and not as the molecule flipping back and forth between them.

Ozone, O3, is the classic example. Total valence electrons: three oxygens contribute 6 each, for 18. A reasonable Lewis structure places a double bond between the central oxygen and one terminal oxygen, and a single bond between the central oxygen and the other terminal oxygen, with lone pairs filling out each atom's octet: the doubly bonded terminal oxygen gets two lone pairs, the singly bonded terminal oxygen gets three lone pairs, and the central oxygen gets one lone pair. Counting electrons confirms the total: 4 from the double bond, 2 from the single bond, plus 4, 6, and 2 from the lone pairs, adds up to 18, and every oxygen has a complete octet.

The problem is that this structure is arbitrary about which terminal oxygen gets the double bond. Swapping the double and single bonds gives an equally valid Lewis structure, obeying the same rules with the same total electron count. Both structures are drawn with a curved double headed arrow between them to show they are resonance structures of the same real molecule, not two different molecules. Experimentally, ozone's two oxygen-oxygen bonds are identical in length, about 128 picometers, which is between a typical single bond, about 148 pm, and a typical double bond, about 121 pm, a strong hint that neither individual resonance structure is the true picture.

Resonance structures only differ in electron placement, never in where the atoms themselves sit. Moving an atom to a new position does not create a resonance structure, it creates a different molecule or an incorrect structure. This distinction connects directly back to Lewis structures and double bonds: you are still applying the same rules for counting valence electrons, placing bonding pairs, and completing octets, but now you recognize that more than one arrangement of double bonds and lone pairs can satisfy those rules equally well for a single set of connected atoms.

Other common resonance examples include the carbonate ion, CO3 with a 2 minus charge, which has three equivalent resonance structures each with one C=O double bond and two C-O single bonds carrying negative charges, and the nitrate ion, NO3 with a 1 minus charge, which behaves the same way. Recognizing when a molecule needs resonance structures, generally whenever you can move a double bond to a chemically equivalent position without changing atom connectivity, is the first step. The next step, covered in the following section, is understanding what the real molecule looks like once you average all of its resonance structures together.
